title: The trumpet
hook: the trumpet is blown, and all rise (39:68)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the questions in the grave, and your line: answer now. Which of the three did a choice of yours answer? Today, the end of the in-between. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

Some sounds end things. A final whistle. A school bell at three. An alarm at six that ends the night whether you're ready or not. The Qur'an speaks of one sound that ends everything, and then starts it again. In Surah az-Zumar, Pickthall's translation reads: "And the trumpet is blown, and all who are in the heavens and all who are in the earth swoon away, save him whom Allah willeth. Then it is blown a second time, and behold them standing waiting!" Two blasts. One to end, one to raise. Today, the trumpet.
screen: `SOUNDS THAT END THINGS.` → `ONE BLAST TO END.` → `ONE BLAST TO RAISE.`

segments.voice: The Arabic is as-sur, a horn. It sounds in more than one surah, here in az-Zumar and again in Ya Sin, in a short, sudden line: and the trumpet is blown. Tradition names the angel who blows it Israfil, though the Qur'an itself doesn't give the name. Look at the verse closely. The first blast brings a swoon over everyone in the heavens and the earth, except whoever Allah wills. Who those exceptions are, the verse leaves open, and commentators have answered in different ways. Then the second blast, and the picture changes completely: people standing, waiting. How long between the two? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, says: between the two blasts is forty. Someone asks him: forty days? He declines to say. Forty months? He declines. Forty years? He declines again. A companion of the Prophet, peace be upon him, who would not go past what he had said. Readers of the hadith take that restraint as part of the teaching. Then Surah Ya Sin gives the moment of waking. When the trumpet is blown, it says, people hurry from their graves to their Lord. And their first words, Pickthall again: "Woe upon us! Who hath raised us from our place of sleep?" The grave, from the far side, felt like sleep. And the answer comes straight back: this is what the Beneficent promised, and the messengers told the truth. So the trumpet is not only an ending. In Muslim teaching it is the sound that means nobody was lost. The verse ends with them standing, waiting.
screen: `AS-SUR: A HORN, BLOWN TWICE.` · `THE SWOON, SAVE WHOM ALLAH WILLS.` · `FORTY WHAT? HE DECLINED TO SAY.` · then, large: `WHO HATH RAISED US FROM OUR SLEEP?`

segments.voice: The practice: think of rising. Sit low, or lie down if you can. Let your body go heavy, as if you'd been asleep a long time. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind the line from Ya Sin: who hath raised us from our place of sleep? Then, near the end of the sit, rise. Slowly. If standing is hard, simply lift your head. Feel your feet take your weight, your spine lift, your head come up last. Stand still for a few breaths. If you pray, you can remember the verse from az-Zumar as you stand. If not, just notice what it feels like to get up. The bell holds the time.
The trumpet. As-sur, the horn blown twice, the Qur'an says: once to end, once to raise. Today's word.
Your line: all will rise. Today, each time you stand up from a chair, let it remind you of the second blast. Tomorrow, the gathering. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims believe the trumpet will be blown at the end of the world and again at the resurrection; the verses that describe it are recited in prayer and in sermons about the Last Day.

fork.setup: you're Abu Hurayrah. you've said: between the two blasts is forty. someone asks: forty days? what do you say?
fork.reveal: he declined three times: days, months, years. he would not go past what he had said.

original.note: Arabic: the horn, or trumpet, of the Last Day.

trapdoor: what you thought: the trumpet is a symbol of doom.
what it means: in the Qur'an it is blown twice: once all swoon, then all stand, waiting.
what a scholar hears: as-sur, the open question of who is excepted, and Abu Hurayrah declining to say forty what.

sources.ref: Qur'an 36:51–52 (from the graves they hasten to their Lord; what the Beneficent promised)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4814 (Abu Hurayrah: between the two blasts is forty)

notes: 'The Qur'an mentions it more than once': confirm.
Israfil as the angel of the trumpet is attributed to tradition; confirm framing.
'Commentators have asked who those exceptions are' (the exception in 39:68): confirm.
Sahih al-Bukhari 4814 (also 4935): confirm number and the days/months/years detail.
Practice asks the listener to stand; those who can't may simply lift the head (already in the practice).

Editor pass: cut 'astonishingly'; 'the Qur'an mentions it more than once' now names the two cited surahs; 'refusing to add a word he hadn't heard' (a motive the hadith doesn't state) reframed as how readers take his restraint, in teach, myth and fork; 'proves nobody was lost. All of them, the verse says' changed, since 39:68 says 'them', not 'all of them'. Versions of the hadith order the questions days/months/years differently; confirm against 4814.
